name: Tokyo
tagline: A thousand worlds in one city.
summary: Temple mornings, tiny noodle counters and neon evenings. Explore one district at a time and save the big cross-city jumps for the train.
seasonNote: Spring blossoms and autumn foliage draw crowds; summer is hot and humid. Blossom timing changes every year.
arrival: From Haneda, use the Keikyu line or monorail with onward rail. From Narita, compare the Narita Express and Keisei routes against your hotel location.
gettingAround: Use rail and metro with a compatible IC card. Different operators share the network; choose your station exit carefully.
cashTip: Keep small yen notes for markets, tiny restaurants and temples; larger shops commonly take cards.
foodTip: Try ramen, soba, sushi and a depachika food hall. At Tsukiji compare posted prices before ordering.
buyTip: Kitchen knives and ceramics in Kappabashi; licensed anime goods in Akihabara. Pack knives in checked luggage.
baseArea: Ueno/Asakusa for older Tokyo; Shinjuku or Shibuya for western districts.

connections.note: Roughly 2h10–2h20 station to station on the fastest services; reserve seats and check luggage rules.
Arrives at Shin-Osaka, with an onward local transfer for Namba or Umeda.

reviewSummary: The retrieved Tripadvisor list puts Senso-ji, Shinjuku Gyoen, teamLab Planets and Meiji Jingu among its leading Tokyo attractions. Ratings are signals, not a promise of short queues or suitability for everyone.

items.name: Senso-ji & Nakamise
items.summary: Start with the great lantern, temple courtyards and an old shopping street.
items.expect: An active temple and busy approach; shops start later than the grounds.
items.tip: Visit the grounds early, then return for ningyo-yaki cakes when shops open.
items.bestTime: Morning
items.priceNote: Free to explore; food and purchases extra.

review.note: Dated indexed review snapshot; review count is a popularity proxy, not measured footfall. Review entity is Senso-ji Temple; Nakamise shops are not separately counted.

whyVisit: Kaminarimon’s giant lantern, a five-storey pagoda and the main courtyard make Tokyo’s Buddhist temple culture immediately visible.
One stop combines active worship with Nakamise’s traditional snacks and craft stalls; the temple grounds are free to enter.
visitFlow: Approach through Kaminarimon and look up at the large lantern.
Walk Nakamise to the incense burner and main hall, following posted worship etiquette.
Explore the quieter side grounds, then return to shops when they open.
items.bestFor: First-time visitors who want traditional Tokyo, architecture and easy food stops.
tradeoffs: Midday crowds are heavy; this is an active temple, and Nakamise is a busy commercial approach.
reviewHighlights: Displayed visitor reviews describe the temple’s scale, fortune slips and charms, and the lively shopping approach as memorable parts of a visit.
Reviewers also describe heavy daytime crowds. Early visits feel quieter, but Nakamise shops may still be closed.
items.reviewHighlightsNote: Themes from displayed individual reviews, including September 2026 examples; this is not a sentiment analysis of all reviews.

items.name: Meiji Jingu
items.summary: A forest approach leads to a Shinto shrine beside Harajuku.
items.expect: Gravel paths, shrine etiquette and occasional ceremonies. Paid gardens or museum are separate.
items.tip: Pair with Harajuku and Shibuya; respect prayer areas and photo restrictions.
items.bestTime: Morning
items.priceNote: Free to explore; food and purchases extra.

review.note: Dated indexed review snapshot; review count is a popularity proxy, not measured footfall.

whyVisit: A long forested approach feels removed from the traffic beside Harajuku.
Shrine gates, gravel courtyards and occasional ceremonies introduce Shinto practice.
visitFlow: Enter through a torii gate and follow the forest path.
Visit the public shrine courtyard respectfully.
Continue to Harajuku after leaving the shrine grounds.
items.bestFor: Travellers seeking a calm green walk with living religious culture.
tradeoffs: The Inner Garden and museum are separate paid experiences; worship photography rules apply.

items.name: Shibuya Crossing & SHIBUYA SKY
items.summary: Watch the crossing from street level, then choose a skyline visit.
items.expect: The crossing is free. The optional rooftop is timed and weather-dependent.
items.tip: Reserve the rooftop separately; check the announced ticketing changes for entry from 19 November 2026.
items.bestTime: Late afternoon / evening
items.priceNote: Planning allowance for optional SHIBUYA SKY. Crossing is free. Rating refers to Shibuya Crossing, not the rooftop.

review.note: Dated indexed review snapshot; review count is a popularity proxy, not measured footfall. Review entity is Shibuya Crossing, not SHIBUYA SKY. Do not present these as rooftop reviews.

whyVisit: The crossing’s simultaneous pedestrian flow makes Tokyo’s density visible at street level.
The separately ticketed SHIBUYA SKY adds a rooftop view over the same urban district.
visitFlow: Cross once from street level.
Walk nearby streets to see the crossing from another angle.
Use a booked SHIBUYA SKY slot only if you want the rooftop experience.
tradeoffs: Crossing reviews do not describe the rooftop; rooftop access is paid and weather-sensitive.

items.name: Kanda
items.summary: Hiroyuki Kanda's counter cooks seasonal kaiseki with Tokushima roots: Naruto fish, Awa beef and local sake, prepared with minimal fuss.
items.expect: A long tasting-menu meal. Deposits, cancellation fees and smart-casual dress codes are common at this level.
items.tip: Book through the restaurant’s own site or official booking partner as soon as your dates are set.

whyVisit: Hiroyuki Kanda's counter cooks seasonal kaiseki with Tokushima roots: Naruto fish, Awa beef and local sake, prepared with minimal fuss.
The MICHELIN Guide awards it Three MICHELIN Stars (exceptional cuisine), the guide’s highest award.
visitFlow: Book through the restaurant’s own site or official booking partner as soon as your dates are set.
Share allergies and dietary needs when booking; tasting menus are hard to change on the night.
Allow about three hours and plan a taxi or short walk back.
items.tradeoffs: Among the most expensive meals of a trip, and tables can sell out weeks or months ahead. Menus are set by the kitchen.
